problem.text: How many strings of length $5$ formed from the digits $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ are there such that for each $j\in\{1,2,3,4\}$, at least $j$ of the digits are less than $j$? (For example, $02214$ satisfies this condition because it contains at least $1$ digit less than $1$, at least $2$ digits less than $2$, at least $3$ digits less than $3$, and at least $4$ digits less than $4$. The string $23404$ does not satisfy the condition because it does not contain at least $2$ digits less than $2$.)

steps.title: Where to start: sort the digits
steps.body:
The condition only counts how many digits are small, so the order of the digits does not matter. Sort them as $b_1\le b_2\le b_3\le b_4\le b_5$. Then "at least $j$ digits are less than $j$" says exactly that the $j$-th smallest digit is less than $j$:
$$b_1\le 0,\quad b_2\le 1,\quad b_3\le 2,\quad b_4\le 3,\quad b_5\le 4.$$

your_turn.answer: $31040$ sorts to $0,0,1,3,4$: yes. $11234$ has no $0$, so $b_1\le 0$ fails: no.

steps.title: Casework on the number of zeros
steps.body: Every good string has at least one $0$. Split into cases by how many zeros there are. The key trick: if there is exactly one $0$, remove it and subtract $1$ from each other digit. You get a length-$4$ string from $0,1,2,3$ that satisfies the same kind of condition, so the problem shrinks.

your_turn.prompt: Warm up with the length-$2$ version (digits $0,1$; need $b_1\le0$, $b_2\le1$). How many strings?

steps.title: Many zeros: the easy cases
steps.body: Five zeros: $1$ string. Four zeros: choose the spot of the non-zero digit ($5$ ways) and its value from $1$ to $4$, giving $20$. Three zeros: $\binom52=10$ ways to place the other two digits, and they must come from $1$ to $4$ but not both be $4$ ($16-1=15$ ordered pairs), giving $150$.

your_turn.prompt: Two zeros: the other three digits come from $1$ to $4$, and sorted they need $c_1\le2$, $c_2\le3$. How many ordered triples work, and what is the case total? (Hint: split by whether a $4$ appears.)
your_turn.answer: No $4$: $27-1=26$ (all from $1,2,3$, not all $3$). One $4$: $3\cdot(9-1)=24$. Two or more $4$s fail. So $50$ triples, and $\binom52\cdot 50=500$.

steps.title: Exactly one zero: shrink the problem
steps.body: Place the $0$ ($5$ ways). The other four digits, each reduced by $1$, form a good length-$4$ string. Count those with the same casework: four zeros $1$, three zeros $4\cdot3=12$, two zeros $\binom42\cdot 8=48$, one zero $4\times$(good length-$3$ strings).

your_turn.prompt: There are $16$ good length-$3$ strings. How many good length-$4$ strings are there, and what is the one-zero case total?
your_turn.answer: $1+12+48+4\cdot16=125$ length-$4$ strings, so $5\cdot125=625$ strings with exactly one zero.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
Add the five cases:
$$1+20+150+500+625=1296=6^4.$$
Notice the pattern: lengths $2,3,4,5$ give $3, 16, 125, 1296$, which are $3^1, 4^2, 5^3, 6^4$. The answer is **(E)**.

wrong_choices.B: $625$ is only the case with exactly one zero (it also equals $5^4$, a tempting wrong guess at the pattern). Check a pattern against small cases: length $2$ gives $3$, not $2^1$.
wrong_choices.A: $500$ is only the case with exactly two zeros. Remember to add all five cases, from one zero up to five zeros.
